World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Live: NT Police providing update on search for missing 5yo Sharon
World.content:
The Northern Territory Police Commissioner Martin Dole will be providing an update this morning on the search for missing five-year-old girl Sharon Granites to ABC Radio Alice Springs.

Live Moment NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole will be speaking to ABC Radio Alice Springs this morning to provide an update on the search for five-year-old Sharon Granites. Police believe people are assisting Jefferson Lewis NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole says he is still adamant that there are people who know information about the whereabouts of Jefferson Lewis. "Our hope is that piece of information comes through, that someone in the community knows something and that they let us know," he said. "There's people out there who are assisting, and that do know something and that aren't feeding that information into the authorities. NT police commissioner speaking to ABC Radio Alice Springs This morning NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole will be speaking to ABC Radio Alice Springs to provide an update on the search for missing five-year-old Alice Springs girl Sharon Granites. Today marks day five of the search for little Sharon, who vanished from a home at Old Timers town camp on the outskirts of Alice Springs. Sharon Granites has been missing since Saturday night. (Supplied: Rob Roy) Police have been treating her case as a major crime, with suspicions that a 47-year-old man named Jefferson Lewis abducted her late on Saturday night. If you'd like to listen to the interview live, you can stream it on ABC Listen, but I'll also be bringing you updates as it airs.

Relatives of missing Alice Springs girl Sharon Granites are all holding onto hope she is still alive, as the search enters a fifth day.

NT Police suspect a recently released prisoner, 47-year-old Jefferson Lewis, abducted the five-year-old from a house at the Old Timers town camp on the outskirts of Alice Springs late on Saturday night.

Sharon Granites was last seen on Saturday night. (Supplied: Rob Roy)

Police have said Mr Lewis was staying at the house where Sharon disappeared, sparking a frantic search that is now entering its fifth day.

Police believe people in the community “absolutely know" where Mr Lewis is, and have urged anyone who may be helping him or know where he is to come forward.

"We believe that there are members of the community that absolutely know where Jefferson Lewis is," Commissioner Dole said.

"What I want to say to you is, tell us.

" Tell us what you know. Tell us where he is. Tell us how to contact him. "

Martin Dole and Peter Malley have provided an update on the search for the missing five-year-old. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Police are looking for Mr Lewis in Alice Springs, Central and Western Australia and have alerted other interstate police forces.

Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said the search for Mr Lewis had been challenging, largely due to his lack of a digital footprint.

""This man doesn't have a telephone, doesn't have a bank account, he doesn't have a car, so some of the usual practices we do in 2026 aren't applicable," he said.

"Hence the amount of resources we have on the ground — we're knocking on doors, we're going through houses.

"It's going back to 1930s policing without that digital footprint."

Police found several personal items at a crime scene at the town camp, which have been sent for forensic testing in Darwin.

Alice Springs community bands together in search for little girl

Loading...

Local residents have continued to turn out in their dozens to help the increasingly desperate search for Sharon.

Parts of the foot search area are overgrown with buffel grass, making the search slow going.

'Only a little baby': Family of missing 5yo Sharon Granites speaks Family members of a missing Alice Springs five-year-old have spoken to the ABC for the first time, pleading for anyone with information that could help find their "energetic" little girl to come forward.

Police have been joined by Defence personnel, Aboriginal corporations, organisations, politicians, community volunteers and everyday residents.

On Wednesday, police said search teams had covered around five square kilometres on foot looking for Sharon.

Sharon's grandfather Robin Granites said his family was devastated, but that police were doing all they could.

He said he was grateful for the community for banding together.

Robin Granites says Sharon is "only a little baby" and her family has been "crying, crying" since she went missing. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"The only thing we can do is being on the sorry business and crying, and that's not what we want, we want to be going out and searching for her, she's only a little baby," he told the ABC.

Police have urged anyone with information to call them on 131 444, or Crime Stoppers 1800 333 000.

What we know about the night Sharon went missing

Sharon and her mother were visiting a home at the Old Timers / Ilyperenye Aboriginal camp on the outskirts of Alice Springs.

Five-year-old Sharon went missing from Alice Springs' Old Timers town camp. (Supplied: NT Police Force )

The town camp is a small community, with only nine households and about 40 residents, which is maintained by the local Aboriginal corporation Tangentyere Council.

Police have said Sharon and her mother were visiting the home of some people they knew well, to do some Saturday laundry.

As the evening went on, police say a party was held at the house for a "social occasion", with several people in attendance.

One of those people was Jefferson Lewis, a 47-year-old man who was staying at the home at Old Timers after having been released from prison six days prior.

History of man police are searching for over 5yo missing girl A man being sought in connection with the alleged abduction of five-year-old Sharon Granites near Alice Springs has a long history of violence and prison time in the Northern Territory.

Police said at 11pm that night Mr Lewis was seen by those in the area for the last time, and he was with a little girl believed to be Sharon.

"He was last seen with the little girl holding hands," police said on Tuesday.

World.title: Prized 'whale vomit' perfume ingredient washes up on WA beach
World.content:
An extremely rare ingredient used in high-end perfume has washed up on a tourist beach on WA's south coast.

The solid waxy material — known as ambergris — is essentially sperm whale vomit or faeces.

It's a highly prized ingredient in the world's most expensive perfumes that takes decades, sometimes centuries, to produce.

An exciting find

Keen fisher Ryan Clarke came upon the rare find on Ocean Beach in Denmark, 415 kilometres south-east of Perth.

At first, the rockmelon-sized chunk looked like a "plain rock".

"But when I actually touched it, it felt completely different than the rock and I knew exactly what it was at the time," he said.

One of the ways to test if it is ambergris is to see if it floats. (Supplied/Ryan Clarke)

"It was hard like a rock surface, but also waxy and very sort of subtle and light to touch, like it was almost weighed like you think a feather would.

"Definitely not what a rock would weigh."

Mr Clarke said he tried to keep a lid on his excitement until he could be sure.

"We did some tests and holy hell, it was ambergris," he said.

Musky, earthy smell

First, he and his wife dropped it into a bucket of water and discovered that, just like ambergris, the substance floated.

Then, they touched its surface with a hot needle, which melted and ejected a "little tarry substance" that quickly solidified and released a "really sweet, musky, oceany, earthy sort of smell in the air".

Mr Clarke said they reported their find to the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions of Western Australia, as required by law, before deciding "really quickly" that they wanted to share it with the community.

"It's such a special find that we didn't want to keep it locked in the drawer somewhere and the community needs to see it," he said.

"It really is a treasure."

What is ambergris?

Marine biologist Pia Markovic said sperm whales mainly eat squid, but squid beaks don't break down in the whale's stomach.

To protect the animal from the hard beaks as they pass through, its insides are lined with a waxy substance.

Mother and baby sperm whale swimming. (Wikimedia: Gabriel Barathieu)

The whale eventually secretes this foul-smelling substance — "whether that comes back out through their mouth or out as faeces" — and over decades, it is slowly cured by the ocean as it floats on the surface.

Why is it used in perfume?

Some pieces float for hundreds of years, with the scent further refining over time.

It's this quality that made it a premium ingredient in perfume in the 1700s, Ms Markovic said, when whalers would harvest about 5 per cent of their catch for the substance.

"It was used in very expensive perfumes for a very long time," Ms Markovic said.

A synthetic version has replaced it as a fixative in almost all perfumes today.

Marine biologist Pia Markovic said the ambergris can come out as vomit or faeces (ABC News: Jon Kerr)

Ambergris is so rare that Ms Markovic only knows of two such recorded finds in WA history.

The piece has been offered to the Museum of the Great Southern where regional manager Catherine Salmaggi, who has been at the museum for 18 years, said she's never seen anything like it.

"This couldn't get any better, really," she said.

Ms Salmaggi said the museum would love to house the rare piece but is in talks with the Western Australian Museum to determine its final resting place.

World.title: Trump's would-be assassin took selfie 'armed to the teeth', court told
World.content:
The man accused of attempting to assassinate US President Donald Trump armed himself with weapons and took a selfie in his hotel room before the attack, court documents say.

Prosecutors revealed further details about the case against Cole Tomas Allen, 31, in documents arguing he should remain in custody ahead of trial.

Mr Allen's lawyers, meanwhile, complained he had been restrained and caged during phone calls with his legal team, with jail staff and other lawyers able to listen in.

Mr Allen is accused of attempting to charge through security into Saturday's White House correspondents' dinner, where prosecutors say he wanted to kill Mr Trump and other administration figures.

His matter is due back in court on Thursday, local time, for a hearing on his ongoing detention.

US President Donald Trump posted a picture of the suspected shooter on social media. (Truth Social: @realDonaldTrump)

The documents, which argue he poses "an uncommonly serious danger to the community if released", suggest Mr Allen had planned the attack weeks in advance.

He had searched online for "white house correspondents dinner 2026" on April 6, according to the documents.

Less than two hours later, he received an email confirming a two-night stay at the Washington Hilton, where the event was held.

'Armed to the teeth'

Ten days later, he used his phone to access "a series of online media articles discussing the Dinner, including its host, the event schedule, and expected attendees".

On the night of the dinner, he looked up the president's public schedule. Then, he accessed live video of Mr Trump exiting his vehicle to attend the dinner.

In between, about 8:03pm, he took a photograph of himself in his hotel room mirror.

He was "armed to the teeth", the documents say. The weapons included a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, a .38 calibre pistol, multiple knives and daggers, pliers, wire cutters and "a significant amount of ammunition".

Cole Tomas Allen was armed with a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun and a .38 calibre pistol, according to the court documents. (Supplied: US District Court for the District of Columbia)

Court documents also allege Cole Tomas Allen was carrying multiple knives and daggers. (Supplied: US District Court for the District of Columbia)

The court documents confirm the text of his alleged "manifesto", which has now been widely circulated. It said Trump officials were his targets, prioritised from highest-ranking to lowest.

About 8:30pm on the night of the dinner, "prescheduled emails" containing the document were sent, the documents say.

"Shortly thereafter, the defendant rushed the screening checkpoint on the Terrace Level of the Washington Hilton with a raised shotgun."

Loading...

Mr Allen allegedly fired "in the direction of the stairs leading down to the ballroom" where the dinner was taking place, the documents say.

Notably, they do not allege that Mr Allen shot a Secret Service agent, as officials had said after the attack.

The documents describe the attack as an "anti-democratic act of political violence".

"Had the defendant achieved his intended outcome, he would have brought about one of the darkest days in American history."

'Forced to sit inside of a locked cage'

Late on Wednesday, Mr Allen's legal counsel filed an emergency motion for a prison visit.

The motion argued Mr Allen had been denied his right to a private consultation with defence lawyers.

This was one of the most vulnerable moments ever for a US government ABC Americas editor was inside the ballroom when a shooting suspect was stopped by the Secret Service.

His legal team had attempted a visit on Tuesday, but were told they would have to meet in "essentially a public location", the motion says.

"Specifically, Mr Allen was forced to sit inside of a locked cage in full, five-point restraints, and speak over a phone — of which there is only one — to be able to confer with counsel," it says.

"Counsel were forced to sit in an open lobby area with jail staff and other attorneys standing nearby who could overhear the entirety of counsel's side of the conversation."

The motion requests that the court order the DC Department of Corrections to permit Mr Allen unfettered access to legal visits in private.

The court has not ruled on the motion.

World.title: NT government accused of hiding long-term watch house detentions
World.content:
The Northern Territory's Aboriginal justice agency has accused the NT government of renaming parts of a Darwin watch house to "mask the fact" that people are still being held there long term, despite repeated government assurances that the practice has ceased.

The NT government's use of police watch houses to hold mostly remand prisoners for weeks at a time has come under intense scrutiny over the past year, with reports of severe overcrowding and "inhumane" conditions.

In November, the NT Ombudsman condemned the practice in a report that said inmates should be removed from watch houses "as a matter of urgency".

NAAJA says the government has renamed parts of Darwin city watch house as a correctional facility to hide its use. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The following month, the NT government announced that almost all prisoners had been moved out of the Territory's watch houses, and that it had committed to reducing reliance on them.

NT Corrections Minister Gerard Maley has repeatedly claimed the Country Liberal Party (CLP) has ended long-term detention in watch houses in the months since.

However, the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency (NAAJA) has now accused the government of renaming parts of the Darwin City Watch House to the Darwin Transitional Custody Centre to continue housing people there for weeks at a time to deal with overcrowding within NT jails.

Ben Grimes says clients have told NAAJA they are being kept in the Darwin Transitional Custody Centre for weeks at a time. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

NAAJA chief executive Ben Grimes said that despite the government's claims, the agency had received contradicting reports from people being detained.

"What it appears to be is that by renaming it from a watch house to a corrections facility and by re-classifying it from a police-controlled watch house to a corrections-controlled facility, it allows the government to say they are not doing what they used to be doing when in fact they are," he said.

"Renaming the facility appears to be the government's way of masking the fact that people are still being held in watch house settings because the government is arresting and remanding more people than our infrastructure can handle."

NT's watch house warning Internal government memos obtained by the ABC detail a series of health incidents in Northern Territory watch houses.

Mr Maley confirmed the Darwin Watch House was being used again, but did not respond directly to questions regarding NAAJA's claims that it had renamed the facility to conceal long-term imprisonments.

He said the facility was now a joint-use site, providing "short-stay, transitional remand accommodation" while also making cells available to police.

"This facility is being used to improve community safety, ease pressure on both police and corrections, and provide additional short-term capacity in a system facing ongoing demand," he said.

Gerard Maley has previously said the CLP government had put an end to keeping people in watch houses long term. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"It also restores a quick CBD drop-off point for police … and gets them back on the streets sooner.

" Claims the government is simply continuing to use police watch houses in the same way criticised by the Ombudsman ignores the significant changes that have been made under the CLP government. "

The government did not provide detailed information about how many people were currently being held in watch houses.

Claims of prolonged detention, overcrowding, no sunlight

Mr Grimes said clients had told NAAJA they were being held in the watch house in small cells with four to five other people for around 23 hours a day, in some instances without seeing the sunlight for "days on end".

"When they're given time outside, it's in an enclosed concrete car park, exposed to vehicle fumes instead of access to fresh air and a proper exercise yard," Mr Grimes said.

Report exposes 'inhumane' conditions in NT watch houses The Northern Territory's prison watchdog has called on the government to urgently remove all inmates from police cells following an investigation which revealed claims guards watched women prisoners showering.

NAAJA said people have also described prolonged detention, no on-site medical staff, and confusion about where they are and what is happening to them.

One client reported he could not tell how long he had been at the facility because he had not seen the sun, while another man said he was kept at the facility for 28 days.

NAAJA said others had complained of "distressingly cold" temperatures and that all clients reported being unable to speak with their families — a deprivation the agency said could be a deliberate decision to prevent the broader community from knowing what is occurring.

Gerard Maley says use of the facility also restores a quick CBD drop-off point for police and gets them back on the streets sooner. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"If the NT government is not being transparent, one of the questions is, what exactly are they trying to hide?" Mr Grimes said.

" The fact that we have a current NT government not meeting basic internationally accepted standards about how we care for people in detention and appear to be trying to hide that fact from Territorians should be of great concern to us all. "

NAAJA is calling on the NT government to commit to transparency about people being held in watch-house-like conditions and to ensure no-one is detained for more than four days.

Mr Maley said the government had delivered 1,004 new beds and repurposed another 274 across the territory's corrections infrastructure in the past 20 months.

"That significant uplift has allowed Corrections to hand back watch houses so they can be used by police for their intended purpose, rather than long-term detention," he said.

World.title: Travis Head makes stunning return to form in IPL
World.content:
Travis Head has made a timely return to form to help Sunrisers Hyderabad to a six-wicket victory over Mumbai Indians.

Head had failed to score a half-century this Indian Premier League (IPL) season before smashing 76 from just 30 deliveries at Mumbai's Wankhede Stadium.

Having opened the batting, Head's knock featured eight sixes and four fours.

One of his sixes flew 99 metres from the bowling of Jasprit Bumrah.

Royals dent crown of Ponting's Kings Ricky Ponting's Punjab Kings record a six-wicket loss against Rajasthan Royals in the IPL, despite Marcus Stoinis's breathtaking innings.

Head, who was dropped three times by Naman Dhir, and Abhishek Sharma (45) combined for an 129-run opening partnership.

The Pat Cummins-skippered Sunrisers overhauled the victory target of 244 with eight balls to spare.

They completed the biggest run chase at the celebrated venue in IPL history.

The Indians made 5-243 after the home side was ignited by Ryan Rickelton's unbeaten 123.

"I definitely thought it was chaseable," Cummins said of the victory target.

"You've got to be realistic now. It's different to what it was five years ago in the IPL.

"Two-hundred [runs] used to be a tough chase. Now, even 12 [runs] an over, you feel like you can chase.

"You've just got to reset your expectations as a bowling group."

Cummins returned the bowling figures of 0-39 from four overs.

It was the second win in a row for Cummins since his return to the IPL.

His team moved one place up to third on the tournament's points table, while the Indians sit in ninth position.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Daughter continues dad's Murray fight as 'transformational moment' looms
World.content:
Julie Jones's house in Clayton, South Australia overlooks the Murray River, where it flows towards the ocean from Lake Alexandrina.

She grew up here, on the last eight kilometres of the Murray, near the dredger keeping the river mouth open.

Julie Jones is continuing her father's fight for the Murray. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She is the daughter of fishers Henry and Gloria Jones who became prominent campaigners when the fight for the Lower Murray was at its lowest point, when the exposed river and lake beds turned acidic during the Millennium Drought.

Even after the flows returned, Henry, Gloria and many in their community remained vocal champions for the region and headed to Canberra as original Murray-Darling Basin Plan was negotiated between the states and the federal government.

Now in her 80s, Gloria Jones is still an active advocate and works with ecologists such as Sylvia Zukowski to reintroduce species. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

'Stand up again for the river'

During that fight in 2012, Ms Jones recalls her father and his mates taking a barbecue and a dingy to the steps of Parliament House to bring attention to the river's plight.

Henry cooked local fish for politicians, listing the species that were extinct while they ate, urging the need for adequate flows for the health of the river in the Murray-Darling Basin Plan.

Henry Jones campaigning at Parliament House in 2012. (Supplied: Julie Jones)

The plan is being comprehensively reviewed for the first time since it was put in place in 2012, but Mr Jones, who died in 2014, will not be here to see it.

His daughter, a Murray-Darling Conservation Alliance River fellow, is calling on South Australians to "stand up again for the river" by taking part in a "transformational moment".

"We're seeing water quality issues and low dilutional flows," Ms Jones said.

"We need this tool [the Murray-Darling Basin Plan] to navigate us through to a better system.

"At minimum, it means reassessing the resource pool, all targets and the allocation frameworks to equally share the risk between users and the environment."

The low level of the Murray was evident at the Goolwa Barrage in 2009. (Supplied: Anne Trebilcock)

Ms Jones said she was concerned by a decision by WaterNSW to halt environmental flows into the Gwydir Wetlands, which led to the death of fish and turtles.

She and her mother took a barbecue and Coorong mullet to Canberra in 2023, along with a petition for the full 450 gigalitres of water earmarked in the plan for the environment to be delivered after it was revealed only 2GL of that amount had been recovered by July 2022.

Gloria and Julie Jones serving Coorong mullet and petitions to politicians at Parliament House in 2023. (Supplied: Julie Jones)

The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said 221.2GL had been recovered as of December 31, 2025.

Wetland worries

While some headway had been made, Ms Jones said the environment was continuing to suffer.

"So far only 26 per cent of the requirements of the Murray-Darling Basin plan have been met. Only four per cent of wetlands are being adequately watered," she said.

Ms Jones said the low flows meant the water was not reaching the South Lagoon of the Coorong and that native species continued to decline.

Dredging of the Murray mouth to enable it to stay open resumed in November 2023. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"It starts with over-allocation, but then you've got the river constraints, you've got stagnant water and then not the right nutrients because the wetlands aren't staying full long enough to create the right biodiversity," she said.

As she looked across to the river from her front deck, Ms Jones explained that the Lower Murray had still not recovered from the Millennium Drought and that it was difficult for the casual observer to be aware of the animals and vegetation that had been lost beneath its brown surface.

Work to restore native species in the Lower Murray is ongoing. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

But she said progress had been made since the inception of the plan.

"We exposed it to Australians that this needs to work in the Northern Basin for the Southern Basin to work, the Murray mouth to stay open and this area needs to have dilutional flows to get rid of the salt and nutrients from the whole basin, not just this area, for the whole basin to work," Ms Jones said.

" We need to give the power back to the river. The river is a living entity. "

Expert backs concerns

Coorong Lower Lakes Murray Mouth Research Centre science program manager Nick Whiterod agreed there had been huge declines in native species in the Lower Murray and Coorong.

Nick Whiterod says Julie Jones has been an "absolute champion" of the river. (Supplied: Nick Whiterod)

"It's difficult because people don't really know the region or know the river," he said.

"They see water and they think, 'Oh, it's all looking OK,'" he said.

Dr Whiterod said the recent listing of the area as critically endangered had highlighted the region's vulnerability.

He said Ms Jones had been "an absolute champion" for the river.

"We need to be listening to people that have the understanding, have lived and worked on the river for decades, and also the science that's being generated," Dr Whiterod said.

Friday deadline

The Murray Darling Basin Authority said it had received more than 600 submissions and that many more were expected before this Friday's 5pm deadline.

"The basin plan was based on the best evidence available at the time," chief executive Andrew McConville said.

"A decade on, we have more data, more experience and a changing climate, so it's the right time to reassess how we manage our waterways and environment."

Murray Watt, senator Charlotte Walker and Penny Wong at the announcement that the Murray and associated wetlands and flood plains downstream of the Darling were critically endangered. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt said in Adelaide this week that the government was committed to delivering the plan "in all its forms".

"South Australians, of all people, understand the importance of delivering the Murray-Darling Basin Plan to protect the ongoing health of the basin and South Australia's water security."

World.title: Six police officers sanctioned over treatment of man who died in prison
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains names and images of First Nations people who have died, and details about suicide and self-harm.

Six police officers have been sanctioned in Western Australia over their treatment of a man in their custody who later died in prison, after the ABC revealed a constable laughed at news of his death.

Linton Ryan died in his cell at a Kalgoorlie prison in April 2025. He was on remand, charged with aggravated assault occasioning bodily harm, after police allege he tried to strangle his partner.

An ABC investigation last year revealed how a constable dismissed Linton's warning that he was going to kill himself.

The officer sent a voice message to a friend after news broke of the 31-year-old Noongar Wongai Adnyamathanha man's death.

Loading...

"I interviewed a man the other day, and he was like, 'I'm gonna kill myself'," the constable said in the recording.

"And I was like, 'yeah whatever'. Put him in the cells. He went to prison the next day and then he killed himself."

The officer signed off the voice message with a giggle, "um, lol", then sent another voice message, "don't tell anyone that".

Linton was transferred to the Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison, where he died in his cell. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

The constable was stood aside while WA Police conducted an internal investigation, prompted by the ABC's enquiries, and apologised to Linton's mother Lynette McIntyre.

WA Police have confirmed the officer has since been given a "managerial sanction", and has resumed work.

"Another five officers, including a supervisor, also received sanctions, in relation to custody procedures," a WA Police spokesperson said.

The revelation of details surrounding Linton Ryan's death sparked an internal police investigation. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

A managerial sanction is a non-disciplinary action taken against officers proven of misconduct to correct their behaviour.

Aboriginal Legal Service of WA (ALSWA) legal services director Peter Collins said the sanctions were inadequate.

"It is entirely predictable that the police involved in the contemptible treatment of Mr Ryan would receive nothing more than a slap on the wrist and effectively given the green light to continue on their merry way," he said.

In a statement, WA Police refuted Mr Collins's assessment.

"The WA Police Force completed a full and thorough investigation into this matter, and appropriate sanctions have been imposed," a spokesperson said.

'I just wish he was still alive'

Linton lived with significant mental health conditions, and had a history of self-harm. While in custody at the police watch house, he had smeared himself with faeces.

An ALSWA lawyer noted Linton had a "very serious" gouge in his arm which had not been medically treated, and he was too unwell to attend his court hearing before he was transferred to prison.

His brother Shannon Smith said the sanctions against the officers were not enough of a punishment, and he believed Linton would still be alive if his pleas for help were acted on.

Linton Ryan's mother and brother, Lynnette McIntyre and Shannon Smith, visit his grave. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"The police should have done a better job. When Linton said he wanted to commit suicide, they should have got help, not laugh about his death," Shannon said.

" I'm scared of the police. I'm scared to have any involvement with the police. "

Shannon said the police officers may never have been investigated, or sanctioned, if details of his brother's time in custody had not surfaced.

"But I just wish he was still alive, and getting help," he said.

WA has highest rates of First Nations incarceration

Mr Collins said the behaviours and attitudes which underpinned the police treatment of Linton Ryan were "deeply entrenched within WA Police".

Aboriginal Legal Service of WA director Peter Collins. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"The relationship between police and the Aboriginal people in this state is at an all time low," he said.

" The treatment Mr Ryan received at the hands of police in Kalgoorlie is no outlier. "

Across Australia, WA has the highest rate of Indigenous incarceration per capita of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Data collated by the Australian Institute of Criminology also showed WA has the highest rates of Indigenous deaths in custody.

Mr Collins said ALSWA's custody notification data showed that almost 50,000 Aboriginal people would be arrested by the end of the year, at the rate of arrests so far.

"There are more Aboriginal people coming into contact with police than ever before," he said.

"There is no appetite whatsoever to change this awful reality."

WA Police said its officers were "committed to serving and protecting all community members in Western Australia".

"[Linton Ryan] was a declared serial family violence offender, as determined by the courts," a spokesperson said.

"The WA Police Force maintains zero tolerance of family violence perpetrators in the community, and will always prioritise the safety of victim-survivors.

"The WA Police Force will always respond to reports of family violence and will investigate and prosecute offenders, regardless of who they are."

World.title: ‘Unprecedented attacks’: Fed chair takes aim at Trump as he vows to stay on board
World.content:
BusinessMarketsTrump's White House ‘Unprecedented attacks’: Fed chair takes aim at Trump as he vows to stay on board Christopher Rugaber Updated April 30, 2026 — 8:21am ,first published 7:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jerome Powell said he plans to remain on the board of the Federal Reserve after his term as chair ends next month “for an undetermined period of time,” saying the “unprecedented” legal attacks by the Trump administration have put the independence of the nation’s central bank at risk. “I worry these attacks are battering this institution and putting at risk the things that really matter to the public,” Powell said in remarks at a press conference after the Fed announced its decision to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged. Jerome Powell decision to stay is the first time a Fed chair will remain on the board as a governor since 1948. Bloomberg Powell’s decision to stay — the first time a Fed chair will remain on the board as a governor since 1948 — denies President Donald Trump a chance to fill a seat on the central bank’s seven-member governing board with his own appointee. The Senate Banking Committee earlier approved Powell’s successor as chair, Trump appointee Kevin Warsh, on a party-line vote. Powell will continue as a Fed governor, possibly until January 2028. Warsh, if confirmed, will take a seat currently held by Stephen Miran, a previous Trump appointee, whose term ended in January. Powell’s move could make it a bit harder for Warsh to engineer the rate cuts that Trump has demanded, and Warsh advocated for last year, economists say.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates ‘Nobody knows’: Trump has left an old foe in the dark Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “It probably means it will take Warsh a little bit longer to build the consensus he is trying to build,” said David Seif, chief economist for developed markets at Nomura, an investment bank. US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said on X Friday that her office was ending its probe into the Fed’s extensive building renovations because the Fed’s inspector general would scrutinise them instead. But she added that her office could reopen the investigation if “the facts warrant doing so.” Apparently that didn’t bring Powell the closure he felt is needed. “I’m waiting for the investigation to be well and truly over with finality and transparency,” he said. “I’m waiting for that and I will leave when I think it appropriate to do so.”



The Fed Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the third straight meeting but signalled it could still cut rates in the coming months, moves that attracted the most dissents since October 1992. Three officials dissented in favour of removing the reference to a future cut, while a fourth, Miran, dissented in favour of an immediate rate cut. The dissents underscore the level of division on the Fed’s 12-member rate-setting committee ahead of the end of Powell’s term as chair on May 15. “Developments in the Middle East are contributing to a high level of uncertainty about the economic outlook,” the Fed said in a statement after its two-day meeting. “Inflation is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices.” Incoming Fed chair cleared a significant hurdle on Wednesday. AP Warsh has promised “regime change” at the central bank and may make sweeping changes to its economic models, communications strategies, and balance sheet. He has argued in favour of rate cuts, as Trump has demanded, but he will likely find it harder to implement them with inflation topping 3 per cent, above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent.



When asked if he believed Warsh would stand up to political pressure from Trump, Powell answered, “He testified very strongly at his hearing, and I take him at his word.” The three officials who dissented against hinting that the Fed may reduce borrowing costs were Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland; Neel Kashkari, president of the Minneapolis Fed; and Lorie Logan, president of the Dallas Fed. The regional Fed bank presidents have historically been more likely to dissent, while the Washington-based governors more often support the chair. ‘I worry these attacks are battering this institution and putting at risk the things that really matter to the public.’ Fed chair Jerome Powell The dissents could renew tension between the Trump administration and the bank presidents, who White House officials have previously criticised. Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said the dissents demonstrated that Fed policymakers are “very independent” and will likely be on hold for months longer. She has forecast a rate cut in December but now isn’t sure. Wall Street investors on average don’t expect a reduction until well into next year, according to futures pricing.



Powell’s decision to stay on could worsen tensions with the Trump administration and would create what some analysts refer to as a “two Popes” scenario, with a chair and former chair both on the Fed’s board. In that case, divisions among policymakers could increase, if some decided to follow Powell’s lead rather than Warsh’s. Powell dismissed the notion that his staying on could cause dissension, saying, “My intention is not to interfere,” later adding that, “I’m not looking to be a high profile dissident or anything like that.” US President Donald Trump has been left frustrated by the Fed’s unwillingness to lower interest rates. Bloomberg Still, Powell said he remained concerned about the Fed’s independence from the White House, which he said is essential to its ability to set rates to benefit the public, rather than in response to political pressure. When the Fed raises or cuts its short-term rate, over time it affects the cost of mortgages, auto loans, and business borrowing. Fed independence remains “at risk,” he said. “We’re having to resort to the courts to enforce our ... ability to make monetary policy without political considerations. We’ve had to do that and we’ve been successful so far, but that’s not over, none of that has concluded yet.”



The unusual situation comes while the economic picture remains unusually murky, putting the Fed in a difficult spot. Inflation has jumped to 3.3 per cent, a two-year high, as the war has sharply raised gas prices. That makes it harder for the central bank to reduce rates. The Fed typically leaves rates unchanged, or even raises them, if inflation is worsening. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve No ‘sock puppet’? What to expect from Trump’s pick for the Fed chair Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the same time, hiring has ground almost to a halt, leaving those without jobs frustrated by the difficulty of finding new ones. Typically, the Fed cuts rates when the job market is weak, to spur more spending and job gains. But layoffs also remain low, as employers appear to be following a “low-hire, low-fire” strategy. Many Fed officials have suggested that as long as the unemployment rate is low, the central bank doesn’t need to cut rates to spur more spending and hiring. Unemployment declined to 4.3 per cent in March, from 4.4 per cent. AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk’: World’s richest person accuses lawyer of trying to trick him in fiery clash
World.content:
Updated TechnologyCourts ‘I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk’: World’s richest person accuses lawyer of trying to trick him in fiery clash Deepa Seetharaman and Max A. Cherney Updated April 30, 2026 — 8:12am ,first published 5:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

California: Elon Musk accused a lawyer for OpenAI of repeatedly trying to trick him during a tense cross-examination at a trial that may determine the future of the artificial intelligence company that built ChatGPT. Musk’s lawsuit alleges OpenAI ditched its mission to build artificial intelligence for the public good, and he is seeking billions of dollars and a change in management and direction for OpenAI, which says Musk knew exactly what was going on and was angry he was not made CEO. The trial highlights the depth of the rupture between Musk and Altman. Bloomberg William Savitt, a lawyer for OpenAI, told Musk his questions about the tax benefits of his $US38 million in donations to OpenAI and the company’s corporate structure were meant to be simple, and that Musk’s responses should be as well. “Your questions are not simple. They’re designed to trick me,” Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, told a nine-person jury in Oakland, California, federal court. The heated exchange came after Musk, over two days of questioning by his own lawyer, accused OpenAI, its co-founder and Chief Executive Sam Altman, and its President Greg Brockman of promising to build a nonprofit to develop AI responsibly, before pivoting to create a for-profit entity in 2019 to enrich themselves.



Related Article Opinion

AI Musk says he’s saving humanity as he battles Altman in court - but it may actually be xAI Elizabeth Knight Business columnist OpenAI has argued that Musk, who helped finance the company’s early growth, is driven by a compulsion to control it and bitterness over its success after he left the board in 2018. It has said he is seeking to bolster his own AI company, SpaceX unit xAI, which lags OpenAI in user adoption. The company also contends Musk pushed OpenAI to become a for-profit business, wanted to become CEO, and that safety was not a priority for him when he was with the company. Savitt asked Musk about an email he sent Altman in 2015 suggesting OpenAI be structured as a for-profit corporation with a parallel nonprofit, part of an effort to show Musk was supportive of a for-profit entity. Musk said the emails did not indicate his definitive position. “Discussions and brainstorming are not a deal,” said Musk, wearing a dark suit over a white shirt and glancing at the jury occasionally as he spoke.



Seated in the courtroom audience, Altman and Brockman - who took notes with a red-ink pen on a yellow legal pad - listened intently as the exchanges between Musk and Savitt grew increasingly heated. Musk repeatedly asked Savitt to stop interrupting him. Musk answered one of Savitt’s questions by saying, “You tell me.” Savitt responded, “I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk.” Musk accused Sam Altman (pictured) and OpenAI president Greg Brockman of not being “honest” about the future plans for the company. Bloomberg Musk is expected to return to the stand for more cross-examination on Thursday. Musk says Altman offer ‘felt like a bribe’



The trial highlights the depth of the rupture between Musk and Altman. The pair co-founded OpenAI in 2015 to create a benevolent steward of the technology and fend off rivals such as Alphabet’s Google. Musk testified he left OpenAI in 2018 to focus on Tesla and SpaceX. The trial comes as OpenAI prepares for a potential initial public offering that could value it at $US1 trillion. AP Microsoft, also a defendant, invested $US10 billion in OpenAI in 2023, a deal Musk said fuelled his concerns that OpenAI was abandoning its mission. Jurors saw text messages Musk and Altman exchanged after news broke of Microsoft’s potential investment. Musk told Altman the move felt like a “bait and switch.” Altman responded, “I agree this feels bad.” Jury sees Altman’s texts to Musk



Earlier on Wednesday, jurors saw an email Musk sent to Altman and Brockman in 2017, referring to himself as a “fool” for providing them funding for what he believed was a nonprofit venture. “What they really wanted to do was create a for-profit where they had as much shareholder ownership as possible,” Musk said under questioning by his lawyer, Steven Molo. OpenAI has said it created a for-profit entity to allow it to accept private investments to help buy computing power and pay top scientists. On cross-examination, Savitt highlighted instances in which Altman appeared to keep Musk apprised of OpenAI’s plans to create a for-profit entity and pursue investment from Microsoft. Savitt asked Musk if he had responded to an April 3, 2019, text message Altman sent him asking, “Do you have a few mins to talk about the Microsoft/openai investment?” Musk said he did not recall if he responded.



Related Article Opinion

AI AI heavyweights’ court battle could unravel the entire sector Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Musk seeks $US150 billion in damages The trial comes as OpenAI prepares for a potential initial public offering that could value it at $USUS1 trillion, Reuters has reported. The company also faces growing competition from rivals, including Anthropic, while a Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI had missed some internal performance targets weighed on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite on Tuesday. Musk is seeking $USUS150 billion in damages from OpenAI and Microsoft, with any award going to OpenAI’s charitable arm. He also wants OpenAI to revert to a nonprofit, with Altman and Brockman removed as officers and Altman removed from the board. His claims include breach of charitable trust and unjust enrichment.



OpenAI is currently structured as a public benefit corporation, in which the nonprofit and other investors, including Microsoft, hold stakes. Reuters Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.content:
CultureMusicMusic awards They’ve got success: Amyl and the Sniffers sweep APRA Music Awards Liz Hobday April 30, 2026 — 7:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punk rockers Amyl and The Sniffers have bagged three top gongs at the Australian music industry’s APRA awards. Jerkin’, the opening track from the band’s third studio album, Cartoon Darkness, has won the prestigious peer-voted Song of the Year award, as well as Most Performed Rock Work. Amyl and The Sniffers receiving the award for Song of the Year during the APRA Music Awards 2026 at Hordern Pavilion. Getty Images The four-piece outfit fronted by high-energy singer Amy Taylor also took home the Songwriter of the Year award for the second year running. “Last time I checked, I’ve got success,” sings Taylor in Jerkin’.



Too right – but it’s one of the very few lines from the high-energy diss track that could be quoted in mainstream media, because the rest are full of swear words. Related Article Obituaries ‘Ferocious and relentless’ Midnight Oil drummer Rob Hirst was band’s power and passion The awards ceremony was held at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on Wednesday night, with performances by Paul Kelly, Christine Anu, Ngulmiya and Rob Ruha. The star-studded evening also celebrated 100 years of APRA, the Australasian Performing Right Association, which was founded in 1926 and collects music royalties for artists. Tributes were paid to the late Midnight Oil founder and drummer Rob Hirst, who died in January at the age of 70.



The Presets performed their version of the Oils’ 1982 hit Power and the Passion, with a guest appearance by Peter Garrett. Related Article Good Weekend From IGA to the ARIAs – via Glastonbury and Gucci: Amy Taylor’s rockin’ rise Sia’s hit track Unstoppable showed it was just that, with the artist winning Most Performed Australian Work Overseas for the third consecutive year. The win means Sia has more APRA awards than any other songwriter, with 14 gongs to her name. The hit track Maybe, by Guy Sebastian and his co-writers Ned Houston and Robby De Sa, took out Most Performed Australian Work and Most Performed Pop Work.



Meanwhile, hit-making songwriter Sarah Aarons, who has worked with K-pop boy band BTS as well as Flume and Tame Impala, took out her sixth APRA gong with an International Recognition Award. World.title: Islamic State-linked families stuck because of Australia’s refusal: Syrian officials
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSyria Islamic State-linked families stuck because of Australia’s refusal: Syrian officials Abby Sewell April 30, 2026 — 7:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beirut: A group of Australian women and children who left a camp in Syria that houses people with alleged ties to Islamic State group militants are stuck in the country because Australian authorities have refused to allow their return, Syrian officials said Wednesday. Thirteen women and children from four families last week left Roj camp, a remote facility near the border with Iraq that houses relatives of suspected militants, on Friday and headed to Syria’s capital. The al-Roj Camp in eastern Syria. AP An official at the camp at the time said that the families were expected to remain in Damascus for around 72 hours and then be sent to Australia. In response to an Associated Press enquiry about their status, Syria’s information ministry said in a statement that after the families left the camp, the foreign ministry was informed that “the Australian government had refused to receive them”.



They were turned back before reaching Damascus International Airport, the information ministry’s statement said. “These families are still awaiting a solution, which can only be achieved through coordination with the relevant international parties.” Loading Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said at a news conference on Wednesday that “we are providing no support for repatriation and no assistance for these people.” At a separate news conference in Beijing, Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong on Wednesday said that her government has made “very clear that we are not assisting in their repatriation”.



Syria’s information ministry said that the families, through a lawyer, had obtained passports that were delivered by an “individual” that it didn’t identify while they were still in northeastern Syria in an area under the control of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF. Related Article Exclusive

Islamic State US government expressed frustration at government ‘opposition’ to ISIS bride repatriation A Lebanese-Australian doctor, Jamal Rifi, previously told Australian media that he was helping to coordinate the repatriation effort. Rifi couldn’t be reached for comment. A previous attempt to return 34 women and children to Australia from the camp in February was turned back by Syrian authorities. Former IS fighters from multiple countries, along with their wives and children, were held in a network of camps and detention centres in northeast Syria after the militant group lost control of its territory in Syria in 2019. Though defeated, the group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in Syria and Iraq.



The larger al-Hol camp has now been closed down, and thousands of suspected IS militants previously held in Syria were transferred to Iraq by the US military to stand trial there. The moves came after fighting between government forces and the SDF in January. Government forces seized much of the territory formerly held by the SDF. Amid the chaos, many detainees fled al-Hol and some prisoners escaped from a detention centre. Australian governments have repatriated Australian women and children from Syrian detention camps on two occasions. Other Australians have also returned without government assistance. World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall as oil surge, Fed drive Wall Street lower; Tech giants’ results Stan Choe Updated April 30, 2026 — 6:49am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street seesawed as investors juggled spiking crude prices and the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate announcement while a quarter of high-profile earnings dropped after the closing bell. The S&P 500 closed flat, the Dow Jones lost 280 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite edged up. The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6.47am AEST pointing to a loss of 61 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.07¢. Wall Street lost more ground on Wednesday. AP The Fed left its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the third straight meeting but signalled it could still cut rates in the coming months, moves that attracted the most dissents since October 1992. Three officials dissented in favour of removing the reference to a future cut, while a fourth, Stephen Miran, dissented in favour of an immediate rate cut. Outgoing Fed chair Powell says he will stay on Fed’s board after his term as chair ends for an “undetermined period of time.” The Senate Banking Committee earlier approved Powell’s successor as chair, Trump appointee Kevin Warsh, on a party-line vote.



Related Article Opinion

Oil Emiratis’ exit from OPEC will boost the flow of oil after the war Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The action was more dramatic in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in July jumped 5.8 per cent to $US110.41 per barrel. It’s where most of the trading is happening in the Brent market, and it got as high as $US111.50 earlier in the day. Oil prices have climbed as President Donald Trump appears willing to keep up the US blockade of Iranian ships, which is preventing the country from making money by selling oil. Iran, in turn, is keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed to other oil tankers hoping to carry crude to customers worldwide as long as the blockade continues. After Wall Street’s closing bell, a number of notable companies released results. Alphabet topped Wall Street estimates for quarterly revenue growth at its cloud computing unit, driven by sustained enterprise spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Shares of the company were up about 4 per cent in extended trading. Alphabet’s total revenue rose 22 per cent to $US109.9 billion in the first quarter, compared with an estimate of $US107.2 billion, according to LSEG data.



Facebook owner Meta Platforms raised its annual capital expenditure forecast, doubling down on its decision to plow billions into artificial intelligence infrastructure even as it seeks cost savings via planned layoffs. Its shares slumped 5 per cent in after-hours trading. Microsoft shares dropped 2 per cent in after-hours trade after posting third-quarter revenue of $US82.9 billion. Amazon shares slid 2.3 per cent in after-hours trade on its results, with total net sales up 17 per cent to $US181.5 billion. Earlier, the US stock market remained largely resilient as more companies joined the procession reporting stronger profit growth for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. Visa jumped 8.3 per cent after delivering stronger results than analysts expected, and CEO Ryan McInerney said consumer spending remained resilient in the quarter. Starbucks climbed 8.9 per cent after likewise reporting better results than expected, while saying customers spent more at each visit, particularly at its North American stores.



Related Article Opinion

AI Musk says he’s saving humanity as he battles Altman in court - but it may actually be xAI Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But those not meeting expectations have gotten punished. GE Healthcare Technologies dropped 13.2 per cent after falling short of analysts’ forecasts. Robinhood Markets tumbled 13.2 per cent after reporting growth in profit that was not as strong as analysts expected. Booking Holdings swung between losses and gains and closed 0.4 per cent higher after the online travel company said the war with Iran is affecting its results and kept some potential customers from booking rooms during the latest quarter. The company behind Booking.com, Priceline and other brands is expecting the conflict to continue affecting its business through the end of June. It could affect travel not only in the Middle East but also in major transit corridors, such as between Europe and Asia. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng jumped 1.7 per cent for one of the world’s strongest moves.

Powell’s decision to stay on could worsen tensions with the Trump administration and would create what some analysts refer to as a “two Popes” scenario, with a chair and former chair both on the Fed’s board. In that case, divisions among policymakers could increase, if some decided to follow Powell’s lead rather than Warsh’s. Powell dismissed the notion that his staying on could cause dissension, saying, “My intention is not to interfere,” later adding that, “I’m not looking to be a high profile dissident or anything like that.” US President Donald Trump has been left frustrated by the Fed’s unwillingness to lower interest rates. Bloomberg Still, Powell said he remained concerned about the Fed’s independence from the White House, which he said is essential to its ability to set rates to benefit the public, rather than in response to political pressure. When the Fed raises or cuts its short-term rate, over time it affects the cost of mortgages, auto loans, and business borrowing. Fed independence remains “at risk,” he said. “We’re having to resort to the courts to enforce our ... ability to make monetary policy without political considerations. We’ve had to do that and we’ve been successful so far, but that’s not over, none of that has concluded yet.”



The unusual situation comes while the economic picture remains unusually murky, putting the Fed in a difficult spot. Inflation has jumped to 3.3 per cent, a two-year high, as the war has sharply raised gas prices. That makes it harder for the central bank to reduce rates. The Fed typically leaves rates unchanged, or even raises them, if inflation is worsening. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve No ‘sock puppet’? What to expect from Trump’s pick for the Fed chair Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At the same time, hiring has ground almost to a halt, leaving those without jobs frustrated by the difficulty of finding new ones. Typically, the Fed cuts rates when the job market is weak, to spur more spending and job gains. But layoffs also remain low, as employers appear to be following a “low-hire, low-fire” strategy. Many Fed officials have suggested that as long as the unemployment rate is low, the central bank doesn’t need to cut rates to spur more spending and hiring. Unemployment declined to 4.3 per cent in March, from 4.4 per cent. AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk’: World’s richest person accuses lawyer of trying to trick him in fiery clash
World.content:
Updated TechnologyCourts ‘I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk’: World’s richest person accuses lawyer of trying to trick him in fiery clash Deepa Seetharaman and Max A. Cherney Updated April 30, 2026 — 8:12am ,first published 5:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

California: Elon Musk accused a lawyer for OpenAI of repeatedly trying to trick him during a tense cross-examination at a trial that may determine the future of the artificial intelligence company that built ChatGPT. Musk’s lawsuit alleges OpenAI ditched its mission to build artificial intelligence for the public good, and he is seeking billions of dollars and a change in management and direction for OpenAI, which says Musk knew exactly what was going on and was angry he was not made CEO. The trial highlights the depth of the rupture between Musk and Altman. Bloomberg William Savitt, a lawyer for OpenAI, told Musk his questions about the tax benefits of his $US38 million in donations to OpenAI and the company’s corporate structure were meant to be simple, and that Musk’s responses should be as well. “Your questions are not simple. They’re designed to trick me,” Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, told a nine-person jury in Oakland, California, federal court. The heated exchange came after Musk, over two days of questioning by his own lawyer, accused OpenAI, its co-founder and Chief Executive Sam Altman, and its President Greg Brockman of promising to build a nonprofit to develop AI responsibly, before pivoting to create a for-profit entity in 2019 to enrich themselves.



Related Article Opinion

AI Musk says he’s saving humanity as he battles Altman in court - but it may actually be xAI Elizabeth Knight Business columnist OpenAI has argued that Musk, who helped finance the company’s early growth, is driven by a compulsion to control it and bitterness over its success after he left the board in 2018. It has said he is seeking to bolster his own AI company, SpaceX unit xAI, which lags OpenAI in user adoption. The company also contends Musk pushed OpenAI to become a for-profit business, wanted to become CEO, and that safety was not a priority for him when he was with the company. Savitt asked Musk about an email he sent Altman in 2015 suggesting OpenAI be structured as a for-profit corporation with a parallel nonprofit, part of an effort to show Musk was supportive of a for-profit entity. Musk said the emails did not indicate his definitive position. “Discussions and brainstorming are not a deal,” said Musk, wearing a dark suit over a white shirt and glancing at the jury occasionally as he spoke.



Seated in the courtroom audience, Altman and Brockman - who took notes with a red-ink pen on a yellow legal pad - listened intently as the exchanges between Musk and Savitt grew increasingly heated. Musk repeatedly asked Savitt to stop interrupting him. Musk answered one of Savitt’s questions by saying, “You tell me.” Savitt responded, “I get to ask the questions, Mr. Musk.” Musk accused Sam Altman (pictured) and OpenAI president Greg Brockman of not being “honest” about the future plans for the company. Bloomberg Musk is expected to return to the stand for more cross-examination on Thursday. Musk says Altman offer ‘felt like a bribe’



The trial highlights the depth of the rupture between Musk and Altman. The pair co-founded OpenAI in 2015 to create a benevolent steward of the technology and fend off rivals such as Alphabet’s Google. Musk testified he left OpenAI in 2018 to focus on Tesla and SpaceX. The trial comes as OpenAI prepares for a potential initial public offering that could value it at $US1 trillion. AP Microsoft, also a defendant, invested $US10 billion in OpenAI in 2023, a deal Musk said fuelled his concerns that OpenAI was abandoning its mission. Jurors saw text messages Musk and Altman exchanged after news broke of Microsoft’s potential investment. Musk told Altman the move felt like a “bait and switch.” Altman responded, “I agree this feels bad.” Jury sees Altman’s texts to Musk



Earlier on Wednesday, jurors saw an email Musk sent to Altman and Brockman in 2017, referring to himself as a “fool” for providing them funding for what he believed was a nonprofit venture. “What they really wanted to do was create a for-profit where they had as much shareholder ownership as possible,” Musk said under questioning by his lawyer, Steven Molo. OpenAI has said it created a for-profit entity to allow it to accept private investments to help buy computing power and pay top scientists. On cross-examination, Savitt highlighted instances in which Altman appeared to keep Musk apprised of OpenAI’s plans to create a for-profit entity and pursue investment from Microsoft. Savitt asked Musk if he had responded to an April 3, 2019, text message Altman sent him asking, “Do you have a few mins to talk about the Microsoft/openai investment?” Musk said he did not recall if he responded.



Related Article Opinion

AI AI heavyweights’ court battle could unravel the entire sector Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Musk seeks $US150 billion in damages The trial comes as OpenAI prepares for a potential initial public offering that could value it at $USUS1 trillion, Reuters has reported. The company also faces growing competition from rivals, including Anthropic, while a Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI had missed some internal performance targets weighed on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite on Tuesday. Musk is seeking $USUS150 billion in damages from OpenAI and Microsoft, with any award going to OpenAI’s charitable arm. He also wants OpenAI to revert to a nonprofit, with Altman and Brockman removed as officers and Altman removed from the board. His claims include breach of charitable trust and unjust enrichment.



OpenAI is currently structured as a public benefit corporation, in which the nonprofit and other investors, including Microsoft, hold stakes. Reuters Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: They’ve got success: Amyl and the Sniffers sweep APRA Music Awards
World.content:
CultureMusicMusic awards They’ve got success: Amyl and the Sniffers sweep APRA Music Awards Liz Hobday April 30, 2026 — 7:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punk rockers Amyl and The Sniffers have bagged three top gongs at the Australian music industry’s APRA awards. Jerkin’, the opening track from the band’s third studio album, Cartoon Darkness, has won the prestigious peer-voted Song of the Year award, as well as Most Performed Rock Work. Amyl and The Sniffers receiving the award for Song of the Year during the APRA Music Awards 2026 at Hordern Pavilion. Getty Images The four-piece outfit fronted by high-energy singer Amy Taylor also took home the Songwriter of the Year award for the second year running. “Last time I checked, I’ve got success,” sings Taylor in Jerkin’.



Too right – but it’s one of the very few lines from the high-energy diss track that could be quoted in mainstream media, because the rest are full of swear words. Related Article Obituaries ‘Ferocious and relentless’ Midnight Oil drummer Rob Hirst was band’s power and passion The awards ceremony was held at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on Wednesday night, with performances by Paul Kelly, Christine Anu, Ngulmiya and Rob Ruha. The star-studded evening also celebrated 100 years of APRA, the Australasian Performing Right Association, which was founded in 1926 and collects music royalties for artists. Tributes were paid to the late Midnight Oil founder and drummer Rob Hirst, who died in January at the age of 70.



The Presets performed their version of the Oils’ 1982 hit Power and the Passion, with a guest appearance by Peter Garrett. Related Article Good Weekend From IGA to the ARIAs – via Glastonbury and Gucci: Amy Taylor’s rockin’ rise Sia’s hit track Unstoppable showed it was just that, with the artist winning Most Performed Australian Work Overseas for the third consecutive year. The win means Sia has more APRA awards than any other songwriter, with 14 gongs to her name. The hit track Maybe, by Guy Sebastian and his co-writers Ned Houston and Robby De Sa, took out Most Performed Australian Work and Most Performed Pop Work.



Meanwhile, hit-making songwriter Sarah Aarons, who has worked with K-pop boy band BTS as well as Flume and Tame Impala, took out her sixth APRA gong with an International Recognition Award. Rock band INXS was recognised with the prestigious Ted Albert Award for Outstanding Services to Australian Music, with performer Ecca Vandal covering the early INXS track Just Keep Walking. 2026 APRA Music Awards winners Peer-Voted Song of the Year: Jerkin’ – Amyl and The Sniffers

World.title: Islamic State-linked families stuck because of Australia’s refusal: Syrian officials
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSyria Islamic State-linked families stuck because of Australia’s refusal: Syrian officials Abby Sewell April 30, 2026 — 7:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beirut: A group of Australian women and children who left a camp in Syria that houses people with alleged ties to Islamic State group militants are stuck in the country because Australian authorities have refused to allow their return, Syrian officials said Wednesday. Thirteen women and children from four families last week left Roj camp, a remote facility near the border with Iraq that houses relatives of suspected militants, on Friday and headed to Syria’s capital. The al-Roj Camp in eastern Syria. AP An official at the camp at the time said that the families were expected to remain in Damascus for around 72 hours and then be sent to Australia. In response to an Associated Press enquiry about their status, Syria’s information ministry said in a statement that after the families left the camp, the foreign ministry was informed that “the Australian government had refused to receive them”.



They were turned back before reaching Damascus International Airport, the information ministry’s statement said. “These families are still awaiting a solution, which can only be achieved through coordination with the relevant international parties.” Loading Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said at a news conference on Wednesday that “we are providing no support for repatriation and no assistance for these people.” At a separate news conference in Beijing, Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong on Wednesday said that her government has made “very clear that we are not assisting in their repatriation”.



Syria’s information ministry said that the families, through a lawyer, had obtained passports that were delivered by an “individual” that it didn’t identify while they were still in northeastern Syria in an area under the control of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF. Related Article Exclusive

Islamic State US government expressed frustration at government ‘opposition’ to ISIS bride repatriation A Lebanese-Australian doctor, Jamal Rifi, previously told Australian media that he was helping to coordinate the repatriation effort. Rifi couldn’t be reached for comment. A previous attempt to return 34 women and children to Australia from the camp in February was turned back by Syrian authorities. Former IS fighters from multiple countries, along with their wives and children, were held in a network of camps and detention centres in northeast Syria after the militant group lost control of its territory in Syria in 2019. Though defeated, the group still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in Syria and Iraq.



The larger al-Hol camp has now been closed down, and thousands of suspected IS militants previously held in Syria were transferred to Iraq by the US military to stand trial there. The moves came after fighting between government forces and the SDF in January. Government forces seized much of the territory formerly held by the SDF. Amid the chaos, many detainees fled al-Hol and some prisoners escaped from a detention centre. Australian governments have repatriated Australian women and children from Syrian detention camps on two occasions. Other Australians have also returned without government assistance.
